title: Console affordance lab notes + wireframe writeups (Apr 2026)
content:
Purpose:
Run lightweight lab sessions to validate two competing affordance patterns for the Console workflow: 1) Inline progressive configuration (single flow) and 2) Modal stepper (explicit steps). Capture usability problems, verbatim quotes, and convert findings into groomed backlog items with estimates.

Date & Setup:
- Sessions: 2026-04-02 — 2026-04-04, remote moderated tests (Zoom + screen share).
- Prototype: mid-fidelity clickable in Figma (iter 4). Two variants A/B: Inline (Variant A) vs Stepper modal (Variant B).
- Participants: 9 product/ML engineers from 6 customers + 3 internal SREs (12 total). Each 45 minutes.
- Tasks: create a model route, pin a model version, configure autoscaling policy, set a canary rollout (10% traffic), and inspect token-cost breakdown for a sample request.
- Metrics captured: task completion (success/fail), time-on-task, System Usability Scale (SUS) quick score, and critical incidents.

Key high-level takeaways:
1) Variant A (Inline progressive) felt faster for experienced users; Variant B (Stepper modal) reduced errors for new users.
2) Major confusion point: where "pin model version" persists across routes vs global model catalog. Users expected persistence at route-level by default; current labels implied global.
3) Costs and latency info are useful when surfaced right after model selection; burying them under an "Advanced" tab led to skipped review.
4) Canary config controls need stronger defaults and clearer safety guardrails (e.g., auto-failback toggle). Several participants accidentally set 100% traffic during stepper flow because the final confirmation used a small font for the percentage input.

Verbatim notable quotes (edited for brevity):
- "I like the inline flow — I can zip through when I know what I want. But if I'm onboarding, I want a checklist." — Senior infra engineer, fintech customer
- "Where does this model get saved? I assumed per-route until I saw a global 'Models' badge in the header." — Platform lead, SaaS company
- "Cost estimates should be a first-class signal, not hidden in an advanced section. I make tradeoffs on tokens immediately after model selection." — ML engineer, adtech

Quantitative summary (aggregated):
- Task success (overall): 87%
- Task success by variant: Inline 92% (n=6), Stepper 83% (n=6) — note small n, paired within-subject design.
- Average time to create + pin route: Inline 5m 50s, Stepper 7m 30s.
- SUS (median): Inline 78, Stepper 72.
- Critical incidents (safety/avoidable failures): 3 (two related to canary misconfiguration, one to ambiguous persistence scope).

Detailed observations and micro-interactions to address:
- Model persistence affordance: users scan for "scope" language. Replace ambiguous phrasing ("Save model") with explicit scope selector (Route / Project / Global) and default to Route for new routes.
- Confirmation prominence: the canary percentage input on the Stepper final confirmation was easily overlooked; increase input size, add a color-coded preview bar showing traffic split.
- Cost/latency preview: insert a compact cost badge next to model versions (small token icon + per-1k estimate) that expands on hover to show latency and quantization variant impact.
- Autoscaling defaults: several users accepted defaults that would under-provision (min=0). Change default min to 1 for Dedicated and surface recommended min based on model profile.
- Error recovery: when a route fails to deploy due to incompatible quantization, current inline error is cryptic. Add actionable remediation steps and a quick-switch to a compatible quantized variant.
- Keyboard shortcuts and copy-to-clipboard: power users asked for quick cloning of routes. Add a 'duplicate route' affordance and Cmd/Ctrl+D shortcut in the route list.

Wireframe-specific notes (sketch-to-implement):
- Route list row: add two inline micro-actions — "Pin model" (hamburger -> quick select) and "Preview cost" (hover reveals cost). Keep rows compact; avoid doubling the vertical density.
- Model selection modal: show model family grouping, version badge, and three-column comparison: (1) inferred latency, (2) token cost estimate, (3) compatibility flags. Allow quick-apply to route from each row.
- Canary editor: timeline-style bar with draggable handles to set traffic slices; inline safety toggles (auto-failback, time window). Provide a canned preset menu (10%, 25%, 50%).

Backlog grooming output (prioritized, with rough estimate and owner):
1) RWI-2037: Add "Scope" selector to model save/pin UI; default Route. (priority: P0, estimate: 3d, owner: product-engineering)
2) RWI-2041: Canary visual editor (draggable bar + presets + auto-failback). (priority: P0, estimate: 8d, owner: eng-serving-runtime + UX)
3) RWI-2055: Cost badge on model versions + hover expansion. (priority: P1, estimate: 2d, owner: product-console)
4) RWI-2060: Change autoscaling default min=1 for Dedicated; add recommendation tooltip. (priority: P1, estimate: 1d, owner: infra-configs)
5) RWI-2072: Error remediation flows for quantization incompatibility (include quick-switch). (priority: P1, estimate: 4d, owner: serving-runtime)
6) RWI-2080: Duplicate route action + keyboard shortcut. (priority: P2, estimate: 2d, owner: console-ux)

Notes on prioritization rationale:
- Safety-first: issues that can lead to misrouted production traffic or accidental 100% canary are P0. Visual clarity that prevents these mistakes was consistently requested.
- Low friction wins: small UI affordances (cost badge, duplicate action) scored high on impact/low-effort.

Research limitations and open questions:
- Small participant pool biased toward engineers; we need a separate test with product managers and security/compliance users to validate persistence language and audit/audit-log expectations.
- Remote moderated tests can miss micro-expressions and hesitation; consider 2 in-person sessions for deeper observation.
- Pricing model complexity: customers with heavy enterprise discounts cared less about per-1k token estimates; we should show both list price and customer's effective price (requires backend signals).

Next steps / action items (owner):
- Asha: file detailed tickets (today) and attach annotated Figma frames.
- Miguel: prototype small visual change for canary input (2 days) and run quick hallway test with 6 internal engineers.
- Rina: sync with infra-configs on default autoscaling min and capture any constraints (by 2026-04-15).
- Tom: schedule follow-up moderated sessions that include PM and Security personas (target late April).

Appendix (sketch links + short notes):
- Figma frames (iter-4): https://www.figma.com/file/abcd1234/console-affordance-iter4
- Raw session notes: internal doc link (Drive) https://drive.redwood.ai/shared_drives/product/console-and-rollouts/raw-session-notes-apr2026
- Short video highlights (redacted): https://drive.redwood.ai/shared_drives/product/console-and-rollouts/highlights/apr2026.mp4

Bottom line: prefer hybrid approach — keep Inline flow for power users, but add optional guided Stepper onboarding mode and stronger visual guardrails around canaries and model persistence. Tackling the three P0 items (scope clarity, canary editor safety, and cost visibility) will remove the most frequent failure modes observed and should be our immediate focus for the next sprint.
